title: Loss-Tolerant Measurement-Device-Independent QKD over Untrusted Repeaters via High-Dimensional Time-Bin Multiplexing
authors: Yu-Chun Yin, Ching-Yi Lai, Alexei Ashikhmin
abstract: We propose a loss-tolerant measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol using time-bin-multiplexed single photons entangled with local qubits stored in nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers. In each round, Alice and Bob each send a single multiplexed photon to an untrusted intermediary, Charlie. Each photon first becomes entangled with Charlie's NV-center qubits; Charlie then performs entanglement swapping between his NV qubits to establish EPR pairs between Alice's and Bob's local qubits. With $d$ time bins per photon, $\log_2 d + 1$ EPR pairs can be generated per transmitted photon, substantially increasing the probability of EPR-pair creation under limited channel bandwidth. To further mitigate the effects of prolonged memory storage, the protocol employs a memory-insensitive (MI) architecture, where multiple banks of qubits and multiplexed photon routing reduce the effective memory lifetime requirements. This approach enhances loss tolerance, enabling higher secret key rates and secure key distribution over longer distances compared to conventional single-photon protocols. Using the Lo-Chau EPR-QKD framework and Shor-Preskill reduction, we prove that the protocol is secure without trusting intermediate nodes, making it suitable for quantum networks with untrusted repeaters.
summary: This work proposes a robust, loss-tolerant MDI-QKD protocol designed for quantum networks with untrusted repeaters. It achieves this by employing high-dimensional time-bin multiplexing to generate multiple entangled pairs per photon and incorporating a memory-insensitive architecture. The results demonstrate a significant enhancement in key rates and transmission distance compared to conventional single-photon methods.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of achieving long-distance, secure quantum key distribution (QKD) over quantum networks containing untrusted intermediate repeaters.
main_result: The proposed time-bin multiplexing protocol significantly enhances key rates and extends the effective transmission distance by nearly doubling it when quantum repeaters are employed, maintaining security against untrusted nodes.
method: The authors combine high-dimensional time-bin multiplexing with an entanglement-based Measurement-Device-Independent QKD (MDI-QKD) framework, incorporating a memory-insensitive (MI) architecture for repeater operation.
model_or_system: The system utilizes single photons entangled with local qubits stored in Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers. The protocol models the generation of multiple entanglement pairs (EPR pairs) per transmitted photon using time-bin multiplexing ($d$ bins).
key_observables: Secret key rate and maximum secure key distribution distance.
important_parameters: The multiplexing factor $d$ (number of time bins), the number of repeaters $R$, and the target key rate.
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes the ability to perform entanglement distillation and relies on the use of NV centers for quantum memory storage.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the three-stage operation of the quantum repeater scheme. Figure 6 compares the performance of the MI $n$-MUX MDI-QKD protocol, showing the distance extension with repeaters.
paper_structure: The paper develops the protocol by first detailing the multiplexing mechanism for entanglement sharing, then extending this to the full MDI-QKD framework, and finally analyzing its performance over a chain of untrusted quantum repeaters.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, high-dimensional extension to quantum repeater protocols, directly impacting the feasibility and scalability of quantum internet infrastructure by improving key rates and distance limits.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Three-stage operation of the n-MUX quantum repeater scheme. (a) Alice and Bob generate n-MUX photons and send them to the intermediate node, Charlie. (b) Successful optical measurements at Charlie herald the creation of entanglement across the elementary links (A–C and B–C). (c) Charlie subsequently performs entanglement swapping on his QMs, thereby distributing end-to-end entanglement between Alice and Bob for subsequent QKD operations.
Fig. 3: Secret key rate ratio rn as a function of the multiplexing depth n at L = 300 km. The ratio falls below unity for n ≥28.

Fig. 4: Secret key rates for the MA n-MUX QKD protocol compared with the conventional 0-MUX protocol, assuming a bandwidth of 2N/(n+1). Dotted lines show the performance of the conventional (0-MUX) protocol under the same band- width constraint as the n-MUX protocol.

Figure 4 as functions of the transmission distance L for various multiplexing depths n. The results in Figure 4 show that using n-MUX photons yields an approximately linear increase in the secret key rate as n grows, while the 0-MUX protocol suffers from reduced performance due to the decreasing available bandwidth 2N/n. For the 0-MUX protocol, the curves corresponding to different n nearly coincide for transmission distances below 60 km. Furthermore, for a fixed multiplexing depth n, our protocol achieves substantially longer transmission distances at the same key rate. For instance, at a rate of 10−4 with n = 7, the n-MUX protocol supports 217.8 km, compared to less than 133 km for 0-MUX....

Figure 5 compares the conventional 0-MUX and 27-MUX protocols. The red solid line represents the 27-MUX protocol, and the red dashed line represents the 0-MUX protocol, showing the higher key rate and longer transmission distance achievable with the n-MUX protocol.
